questions.question: The eigen values of the matrix \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] are
questions.explanation: Given the determinant: \[\begin{vmatrix} 2 - \lambda & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 - \lambda & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 - \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 4 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[\Rightarrow (2 - \lambda) \begin{vmatrix} 3 - \lambda & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 - \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[\Rightarrow (2 - \lambda) (3 - \lambda) [(-2 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) - 0] = 0\] \[\Rightarrow (2 - \lambda) (3 - \lambda) [-(2 + \lambda)(4 - \lambda)] = 0\] \[\Rightarrow (2 - \lambda) (3 - \lambda) (2 + \lambda) (4 - \lambda) = 0\] Solving for \(\lambda\), we get: \[\lambda = 2, 3, -2, 4\] The eigenvalues of the matrix are \(2, -2, 3,\) and \(4\). \[\boxed{\text{(B) 2, 3, -2, 4}}\]

questions.question: In Figure, the steady state output voltage corresponding to the input voltage 3+ 4 sin 100t V is
questions.explanation: Let us find the transfer function of this network. The network is a simple first order low pass filter with transfer function \(H(s) = \frac{1}{sRC + 1}\), where \(R=1\,k\Omega\) and \(C = 10 \mu F\). \[\therefore, H(s) = \frac{1}{0.01s+1}=\frac{100}{s+100}\] By principle of superposition, we need to investigate the output at two frequencies as per given input, i.e. at dc and at 100 rad/sec. For a dc input of magnitude 3V, the capacitor would eventually charge upto 3V. Hence the output for the 3V input would be 3V itself. Next to investigate for the input 4 sin 100t V, we need to check the frequency reponse for 100 rad/sec frequency. \[|H(\omega)|=\frac{100}{j100+100}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\angle-45^{\circ}\] We know, \[|V_o(j\omega)|=|H(\omega)||V_i(\omega)| \,\textit{and}\, \angle V_o(j\omega)=\angle H(\omega)+\angle V_i(\omega)\] \[\therefore |V_o(j\omega)| = 4\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\,\textit{and}  \angle V_o(j\omega)=0^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=-45^{\circ}\] Thus in time domain, \[V_o(t)= \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\sin{(100t-\frac{\pi}{4})}\] Combining both outputs, \(V_o(t)= 3+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\sin{(100t-\frac{\pi}{4})}\) V \[\boxed{(a)3+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\sin{(100t-\frac{\pi}{4})} V}\]

questions.question: For the circuit in Figure, which is in steady state (a) Find the frequency \(\omega_o\) at which the magnitude of the impedance across terminals a and b reaches a maximum. (b)Find the impedance across a,b at the frequency \(\omega_o\). (c) If \(v_i(t)=V\sin(\omega_ot),\) find \(i_L(t)\), \(i_C(t)\) and \(i_R(t)\)
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: Impedance across terminal \(a\) & \(b\) will be maximum when the parallel RLC circuit is in resonance because in a parallel RLC circuit, impedance is maximum at resonance frequency. The admittance \(Y_1\) of the parallel RLC combination is given by: \[Y_1 = \frac{1}{j\omega_0 L} + \frac{1}{\frac{1}{j\omega_0 C}} + \frac{1}{R}\] Substituting the given values from the circuit parameters (\(L = 4\,\text{H}\), \(C = 4\,\text{F}\)): \[Y_1 = \frac{1}{j\omega_0 \cdot 4} + j\omega_0 \cdot 4 + \frac{1}{R} = \frac{-j}{4\omega_0} + j\omega_0 \cdot 4 + \frac{1}{R}\] \[Y_1 = \frac{1}{R} + j\left[4\omega_0 - \frac{1}{4\omega_0}\right]\] At resonance, the imaginary part of admittance must be zero (\(\text{Im}(Y_1) = 0\)): \[4\omega_0 = \frac{1}{4\omega_0}\] \[\omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{16} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{4}\,\text{rad/sec} = 0.25\,\text{rad/sec}\] (b) Finding Total Impedance At resonance frequency \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{4}\,\text{rad/sec}\): \[Y_1 = \frac{1}{R} \implies Z_1 = R = 2\,\Omega\] The total impedance \(Z_{\text{th}}\) across the terminals is the sum of the series resistor and the resonant tank circuit impedance: \[Z_{\text{th}} = 2 + 2 = 4\,\Omega\] Hence, the value is 4. (c) Finding Time-Domain Currents Given input voltage: \[V_i(t) = V\sin(\omega_0 t) = V\sin(0.25t)\,\text{V}\] At resonance \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{4}\,\text{rad/sec}\), by voltage division, the voltage across the parallel combination \(V_c(t)\) is: \[V_c(t) = V_i(t) \times \frac{2}{2+2} = \frac{V}{2}\sin(0.25t)\,\text{V}\] Now, calculating individual branch currents in time-domain: 1. Capacitor Current \(i_C(t)\): \[i_C(t) = V_c(t) \times 4j\omega_0 = \frac{V}{2}\sin(0.25t) \times 4 \times \frac{1}{4} \times j\] \[i_C(t) = \frac{V}{2}\sin(0.25t + 90^\circ) = \frac{V}{2}\cos(0.25t)\,\text{A}\] 2. Resistor Current \(i_R(t)\): \[i_R(t) = \frac{V_c(t)}{2} = \frac{V}{4}\sin(0.25t)\,\text{A}\] 3. Inductor Current \(i_L(t)\): \[i_L(t) = \frac{V_c(t)}{4j\omega_0} = \frac{-j V\sin(0.25t)}{2 \times 4 \times \frac{1}{4}}\] \[i_L(t) = -\frac{V}{2}\cos(0.25t)\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{(a)\omega_0= 0.25\,\text{rad/sec},(b) Z_{\text{th}} = 4\,\Omega, (c)i_L(t) = -\frac{V}{2}\cos(0.25t)\,\text{A} }\]

questions.question: A system with an input \(x(t)\) and output \(y(t)\) is described by the relation: \(y(t) = tx(t)\). This system is
questions.explanation:
To determine the properties of the system \(y(t) = t x(t)\), we evaluate it for linearity and time-invariance. 1. Linearity Check
Let \(x_{1}(t)\) and \(x_{2}(t)\) be two inputs, producing outputs \(y_{1}(t) = t x_{1}(t)\) and \(y_{2}(t) = t x_{2}(t)\) respectively. For a linear combination of inputs \(x_{3}(t) = a x_{1}(t) + b x_{2}(t)\), the output is: \[y_{3}(t) = t x_{3}(t) = t [a x_{1}(t) + b x_{2}(t)]\] \[y_{3}(t) = a [t x_{1}(t)] + b [t x_{2}(t)] = a y_{1}(t) + b y_{2}(t)\] Since the system satisfies the superposition principle, it is linear. 2. Time-Invariance Check
Let the input be delayed by \(t_{0}\), so the new input is \(x_{1}(t) = x(t - t_{0})\). The output due to this delayed input is: \[y_{1}(t) = t x_{1}(t) = t x(t - t_{0})\] Now, delaying the original output \(y(t)\) by \(t_{0}\) yields: \[y(t - t_{0}) = (t - t_{0}) x(t - t_{0})\] Comparing the two expressions, we observe: \[y_{1}(t) \neq y(t - t_{0})\] Since a time shift in the input does not result in an identical time shift in the output, the system is time-varying. Therefore, the system is linear and time-varying. \[\boxed{\text{B) Linear and time varying }}\]
Key points
  • A system is linear if it satisfies additivity and homogeneity (the superposition principle).
  • A system is time-invariant if an output \(y_{1}(t)\) due to a delayed input \(x(t - t_{0})\) equals the delayed output \(y(t - t_{0})\).
  • Multiplying a signal by the time variable \(t\) introduces a time-varying property.

questions.explanation:
\(W_{1}\) is a periodic square waveform with period \(T\) and it is having odd symmetry and also odd harmonic symmetry (or Half-wave symmetry). \(W_{2}\) is a periodic triangular waveform with period \(T\) and it is having odd symmetry and also odd harmonic symmetry (or Half-wave symmetry). \(\therefore\) Only odd harmonics: \(n f_{0}\), \(n = 1, 3, 5\) etc. of sine terms are present in wave forms \(W_{1}\) and \(W_{2}\) in their Fourier series expansion. Note that waveform, \(W_{2}\) can be obtained by integrating the waveform, \(W_{1}\). If \(C_{n}\) is the exponential FS coefficient of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) harmonic component, \[|C_{n}| \propto \left| \frac{1}{n} \right| = |n^{-1}| \quad \text{for waveform } W_{1}\] \[|C_{n}| \propto \left| \frac{1}{n^{2}} \right| = |n^{-2}| \quad \text{for waveform } W_{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) $|n^{-1}|$ and $|n^{-2}|$ }}\]
Key points
  • A waveform with both odd symmetry and odd harmonic (half-wave) symmetry contains only odd harmonic sine terms in its Fourier series expansion.
  • The magnitude of the Fourier series coefficients for a square wave decays at a rate proportional to \(1/n\).
  • Integrating a signal in the time domain corresponds to dividing its Fourier coefficients by \(jn\omega_{0}\), meaning the coefficients of the resulting triangular wave decay at a rate proportional to \(1/n^{2}\).

questions.question: The Fourier Transform of the signal \(x(t) = e^{-3t^2}\) is of the following form, where A and B are constants:
questions.explanation:
The given signal is: \[x(t) = e^{-3t^2}\] This is a Gaussian pulse of the general form \(e^{-\alpha t^2}\), where \(\alpha = 3\). The standard Fourier Transform pair for a Gaussian function is known to be: \[\mathcal{F} \left\{ e^{-\alpha t^2} \right\} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}} e^{-\frac{\pi^2 f^2}{\alpha}}\] Substituting \(\alpha = 3\) into the standard formula, we obtain the Fourier Transform \(X(f)\) of the given signal: \[X(f) = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^{-\frac{\pi^2 f^2}{3}}\] We can express this result in terms of constants by defining: \[A = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}} \quad \text{and} \quad B = \frac{\pi^2}{3}\] Substituting these constants back into our expression for \(X(f)\) gives: \[X(f) = A e^{-B f^2}\] This form exactly matches the expression provided in option D. \[\boxed{\text{D) $Ae^{-Bf^2}$ }}\]
Key points
  • Gaussian Pulse Properties: A signal of the form \(e^{-\alpha t^2}\) is called a Gaussian pulse.
  • Invariant Shape: The Gaussian pulse is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. This means that its Fourier transform results in another Gaussian pulse; it retains its bell-curve shape in both the time domain and the frequency domain.
  • A wider pulse in the time domain (smaller \(\alpha\)) corresponds to a narrower pulse in the frequency domain, demonstrating the time-bandwidth product principle.

questions.question: The Hilbert transform of \([\cos \omega_1 t + \sin \omega_2 t]\) is
questions.explanation:
The Hilbert transform is a linear operation that imparts a \(-90^\circ\) (\(-\frac{\pi}{2}\)) phase shift to all positive frequency components of a signal. Given the signal: \[x(t) = \cos(\omega_1 t) + \sin(\omega_2 t)\] Because the Hilbert transform, denoted by \(H[\cdot]\), is a linear operator, we can apply it to each term independently: \[H[x(t)] = H[\cos(\omega_1 t)] + H[\sin(\omega_2 t)]\] Using the standard Hilbert transform pairs for sinusoidal functions: \[H[\cos(\omega t)] = \cos\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin(\omega t)\] \[H[\sin(\omega t)] = \sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\cos(\omega t)\] Applying these transform pairs to our specific signal components: \[H[x(t)] = \sin(\omega_1 t) - \cos(\omega_2 t)\] This exactly matches option A. \[\boxed{\text{A) $\sin \omega_1 t - \cos \omega_2 t$ }}\]
Key points
  • Linearity: \(H[a x_1(t) + b x_2(t)] = a H[x_1(t)] + b H[x_2(t)]\).
  • Phase Shift: The Hilbert transform corresponds to an LTI system with a magnitude response \(|H(f)| = 1\) and a phase response \(\angle H(f) = -90^\circ\) for \(f > 0\) and \(+90^\circ\) for \(f < 0\).
  • Standard Pairs: It is essential to remember the fundamental relationships: \(H[\cos(\omega_c t)] = \sin(\omega_c t)\) and \(H[\sin(\omega_c t)] = -\cos(\omega_c t)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • A common error is incorrectly assuming \(H[\sin(\omega t)] = \cos(\omega t)\) by confusing the phase shift of the Hilbert transform with standard time differentiation. Always remember the negative sign for the sine transform!

L[g(t)] = \frac{s^2+1}{(s+3)(s+2)}\] and \[h(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau)g(t-\tau)\,d\tau.\] Then, \(L[h(t)]\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the Laplace transforms from the problem description: \[F(s) = L[f(t)] = \frac{s + 2}{s^2 + 1}\] Note: The problem image contains a typo, stating \(L[f(t)]\) twice. The second function is assumed to be \(L[g(t)]\) based on the convolution integral provided. \[G(s) = L[g(t)] = \frac{s^2 + 1}{(s + 3)(s + 2)}\] The given integral represents the convolution of \(f(t)\) and \(g(t)\): \[h(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau)g(t-\tau)d\tau = f(t) * g(t)\] According to the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms, the transform of a convolution in the time domain is the product of their individual Laplace transforms in the \(s\)-domain: \[L[h(t)] = L[f(t) * g(t)] = F(s) \cdot G(s)\] Substituting the given expressions into the equation: \[L[h(t)] = \left( \frac{s + 2}{s^2 + 1} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{s^2 + 1}{(s + 3)(s + 2)} \right)\] Canceling the common terms \((s+2)\) and \((s^2+1)\): \[L[h(t)] = \frac{1}{s + 3}\] \[\boxed{B)\frac{1}{s + 3}}\]
Key points
  • The convolution of two functions \(f(t)\) and \(g(t)\) is defined as \(f(t) * g(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau)g(t-\tau)d\tau\).
  • The Convolution Theorem states that the Laplace transform of the convolution of two functions is the algebraic product of their individual Laplace transforms: \(L[f(t) * g(t)] = F(s) \cdot G(s)\).

questions.question: A linear time invariant system has an impulse response \(e^{2t}\), \(t > 0\). If the initial conditions are zero and the input is \(e^{3t}\), then output for \(t > 0\) is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Using Laplace Transform
Given the impulse response \(h(t) = e^{2t}\) and input \(x(t) = e^{3t}\) for \(t > 0\). Taking the Laplace transform of both signals: \[H(s) = \frac{1}{s-2}\] \[X(s) = \frac{1}{s-3}\] For a linear time invariant (LTI) system with zero initial conditions, the output in the s-domain is given by \(Y(s) = X(s)H(s)\): \[Y(s) = \left(\frac{1}{s-3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{s-2}\right)\] Using partial fraction expansion: \[Y(s) = \frac{1}{s-3} - \frac{1}{s-2}\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform, we get the time domain output: \[y(t) = e^{3t} - e^{2t}\]
Method 2
Using Convolution Integral
The output \(y(t)\) of an LTI system is the convolution of its input \(x(t)\) and impulse response \(h(t)\): \[y(t) = \int_{0}^{t} x(\tau) h(t-\tau) \, d\tau\] Substituting the given functions: \[y(t) = \int_{0}^{t} e^{3\tau} e^{2(t-\tau)} \, d\tau\] \[y(t) = e^{2t} \int_{0}^{t} e^{3\tau} e^{-2\tau} \, d\tau = e^{2t} \int_{0}^{t} e^{\tau} \, d\tau\] \[y(t) = e^{2t} \left[ e^{\tau} \right]_{0}^{t} = e^{2t} (e^{t} - 1)\] \[y(t) = e^{3t} - e^{2t}\] \[\boxed{\text{A) }e^{3t} - e^{2t}}\]
Key points
  • The output of an LTI system is given by the convolution of the input and the impulse response: \(y(t) = x(t) * h(t)\).
  • In the Laplace domain, convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication: \(Y(s) = X(s)H(s)\).
  • The standard Laplace transform pair: \(\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}u(t)\} = \frac{1}{s-a}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Forgetting that the limits of integration for causal signals (\(t > 0\)) are from \(0\) to \(t\), rather than \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\).
  • Making sign errors during the partial fraction expansion step.

questions.question: If the op-amp in figure, has an input offset voltage of \(5\,\text{mV}\) and an open-loop voltage gain of \(10,000\), then \(V_o\) will be
questions.explanation:
Given, Input offset voltage, \(V_{ios} = 5\,\text{mV}\) Open loop voltage gain, \(A_{OL} = 10000\) Given circuit is shown below,
Method 1
Open loop gain, \(A_{OL} = \frac{V_0}{V_d}\) \[A_{OL} \neq \infty \quad \text{i.e.} \quad V_d \neq 0\] \[V_d = V_{NI} - V_I\] Case 1 :
If \(V_{NI} = V_{ios}\) , then \(V_I = 0\) \[V_d = V_{ios} - V_I = 5\,\text{mV} - 0\] \[V_d = 5\,\text{mV} \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] Case 2 :
If \(V_I = V_{ios}\) , then \(V_{NI} = 0\) \[V_d = V_{NI} - V_{ios} = 0 - 5\,\text{mV}\] \[V_d = -5\,\text{mV} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] From case 1 and case 2, differential input voltage \(V_d\) can be written as given below, \[V_d = \pm 5\,\text{mV}\] Output voltage is given by, \[V_0 = A_{OL}V_d\] \[V_0 = 10000 \times (\pm 5\,\text{mV}) = \pm 50\,\text{V}\] But output voltage cannot be greater than saturation voltage. Therefore, \(V_0 = \pm 15\,\text{V}\)
Method 2
Output voltage \(V_0 = A_{OL} \times V_{ios}\) \[V_0 = 10^4 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}\] \[V_0 = 50\,\text{V}\] Since, in Open loop Op-Amp, output can not be greater than \(\pm V_{sat}\) . Therefore output voltage will be \(+V_{sat} (=15\,\text{V})\) or \(-V_{sat} (=-15\,\text{V})\) .
\[\boxed{\text{(C)}+15\,\text{V}\text{ or }-15\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • Input Offset Voltage (\(V_{ios}\)): The small internal mismatch in the differential input stage, modeled as a small DC voltage source in series with one of the input terminals. Its exact polarity is usually unknown, hence the \(\pm\) consideration.

questions.question: For the logic circuit shown in figure, the simplified Boolean expression for the output \(Y\) is
questions.explanation:
From the given logic circuit diagram, let us label the intermediate outputs of the gates sequentially to find the expression for the final output \(Y\).
Method 1
Let us trace and simplify the Boolean expressions at each gate output stage from left to right:
  • Stage 1 (First NAND gate):
    \[P = \overline{A \cdot B}\]
  • Stage 2 (Second NAND gate with a bubbled input from \(P\)):
    \[Q = \overline{P \cdot \overline{B}} = \overline{P} + \overline{\overline{B}} = \overline{P} + B\] Substituting \(\overline{P} = \overline{\overline{A \cdot B}} = AB\): \[Q = AB + B = B(A+1)=B\]
  • Stage 3 (Third NAND gate with inputs \(Q\) and \(B\)):
    \[R = \overline{Q \cdot B} = \overline{B \cdot B} = \overline{B}\]
  • Stage 4 (NOR gate with a normal input from \(Q\) and bubbled input from \(C\)):
    \[S = \overline{Q + \overline{C}} = \overline{Q} \cdot C\] Substituting \(Q = B\): \[S = \overline{B} \cdot C\]
  • Stage 5 (Final NOR gate with inputs \(R\) and \(S\)):
    \[Y = \overline{R + S} = \overline{\overline{B} + \overline{B} \cdot C} = \overline{\overline{B}(1 + C)} = \overline{\overline{B}} = B\]
\[Y = B\]
Method 2
Using bubble shifting rules (De Morgan's equivalent graphic representation): By shifting the output inversion bubbles forward onto the inputs of the succeeding stages:
  • Bubbled NAND Gate is equivalent to an OR Gate:
    By applying De Morgan's Theorem, \[\text{Output} = \overline{\overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}} = \overline{\overline{A}} + \overline{\overline{B}} = A + B\] This matches the Boolean expression for a standard two-input OR gate.
  • Bubbled NOR Gate is equivalent to an AND Gate:
    Applying De Morgan's Theorem, \[\text{Output} = \overline{\overline{A} + \overline{B}} = \overline{\overline{A}} \cdot \overline{\overline{B}} = A \cdot B\] This matches the Boolean expression for a standard two-input AND gate.
Combining the signals at the final gate stage yields: \[Y = B \cdot (B + \overline{C}) = B \cdot B + B\overline{C} = B(1+\overline{C})=B\] When resolved through the output NOR block matching the diagram configuration, it simplifies uniquely to: \[Y = B\]
\[\boxed{\text{(C) } B}\]

questions.question: For the logic circuit shown in Figure, the required input condition \((A, B, C)\) to make the output \((X) = 1\) is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The output \(X\) of the given logic circuit is, To make the output \(X = 1\), all inputs to the AND gate must be at logic 1. This gives us three simultaneous conditions:
  • \(C = 1\)
  • \(B \odot C = 1\) For \(B \odot C = 1\). An XNOR gate outputs \(1\) only when both of its inputs are identical. Since \(C = 1\), it follows that \(B = 1\).
  • \(A \oplus B = 1\) For \(A \oplus B = 1\). An XOR gate outputs \(1\) only when its inputs are different. Given \(B = 1\), it must be that \(A = 0\).
Thus, the required input condition is \((A, B, C) = (0, 1, 1)\).
Method 2
Alternatively, we can evaluate the Boolean expression \(X = (A \oplus B) \cdot (B \odot C) \cdot C\) for each given option to see which one results in \(X = 1\):
  • (A) 1, 0, 1: \(X = (1 \oplus 0) \cdot (0 \odot 1) \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 1 = 0\)
  • (B) 0, 0, 1: \(X = (0 \oplus 0) \cdot (0 \odot 1) \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 0 \cdot 1 = 0\)
  • (C) 1, 1, 1: \(X = (1 \oplus 1) \cdot (1 \odot 1) \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 0\)
  • (D) 0, 1, 1: \(X = (0 \oplus 1) \cdot (1 \odot 1) \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1\)
Only option (D) satisfies the condition \(X = 1\).
\[\boxed{\text{(D) } 0, 1, 1}\]
Key points
  • AND Gate: Output is 1 if and only if all inputs are 1.
  • XOR Gate (\(\oplus\)): Output is 1 when inputs are different (\(A \neq B\)).
  • XNOR Gate (\(\odot\)): Output is 1 when inputs are identical (\(A = B\)).

It is required that the indicator (LED) on the panel should glow when a majority of the pumps fail.

The above expression is implemented using logic gates, and point \(P\) is the output of this circuit, as shown in Figure \(P\) is at \(0\text{ V}\) when a majority of the pumps fails and is at \(5\text{ V}\) otherwise. Design a circuit to drive the LED using this output. The current through the LED should be \(10\text{ mA}\) and the voltage drop across it is \(1\text{ V}\). Assume that \(P\) can source or sink \(10\text{ mA}\) and a \(5\text{ V}\) supply is available.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given specifications for driving the LED:
  • When a majority of pumps fail: Point \(P = 0\,\text{V}\) (Logic 0).
  • Otherwise: Point \(P = 5\,\text{V}\) (Logic 1).
  • LED forward current: \(I_{\text{LED}} = 10\,\text{mA} = 10 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{A}\).
  • LED forward voltage drop: \(V_{\text{LED}} = 1\,\text{V}\).
  • Available DC supply voltage: \(V_{CC} = 5\,\text{V}\).
When a majority of the pumps fail, \(P = 0\,\text{V}\), and the LED must turn ON (glow). This dictates a current-sinking configuration, where the LED is connected between the \(5\,\text{V}\) source and the output terminal \(P\). Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) through the LED path when \(P = 0\,\text{V}\): \[V_{CC} - V_{\text{LED}} - I_{\text{LED}} \cdot R = V_P\] \[5\,\text{V} - 1\,\text{V} - (10 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{A}) \cdot R = 0\,\text{V}\] \[4\,\text{V} = 10^{-2} \cdot R\] \[R = \frac{4}{10^{-2}} = 400\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{R = 400\,\Omega \text{ in current-sinking mode}}\]

questions.question: In Figure, the \(J\) and \(K\) inputs of all the four Flip-Flops are made high. The frequency of the signal at output \(Y\) is
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is a negative edge-triggered asynchronous counter. Since the clock of each subsequent flip-flop is connected to the \(Q\) output of the previous flip-flop, it operates as an **up counter**. The clear input (\(\overline{\text{CLR}}\)) is controlled by a NAND gate whose inputs are connected to \(Q_3\) and \(Q_1\). Thus: \[\overline{\text{CLR}} = \overline{Q_3 Q_1}\] The counter resets to \(0000\) immediately when \(Q_3 = 1\) and \(Q_1 = 1\) (i.e., when the state reaches \(1010_2 = 10_{10}\)). Therefore, the valid counting states are from \(0000\) to \(1001\) (\(0\) to \(9\) in decimal), making it a **MOD-10 counter**. The frequency of the output signal \(Y\) (which is \(Q_3\)) is given by: \[f_{out} = \frac{f_{\text{CLK}}}{\text{Modulus of the counter}}\] \[f_{out} = \frac{10\,\text{kHz}}{10} = 1.0\,\text{kHz}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\; 1.0\,\text{kHz}}\]
Key points
  • For an asynchronous up-counter using negative edge-triggered flip-flops, the clock input of the next stage is driven by the \(Q\) output of the preceding stage.
  • The modulus of a counter with a feedback clearing circuit is equal to the decimal equivalent of the state that triggers the clear condition.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the transient state (\(1010\)) as a stable counting state. The counter only stays in this state for a negligible propagation delay before resetting.

questions.question: A sequential circuit using D flip-flop and logic gates is shown in Figure, where \(X\) and \(Y\) are the inputs and \(Z\) is the output. The circuit is
options: \(S-R\) Flip-Flop with inputs \(X = R\) and \(Y = S\)
\(S-R\) Flip-Flop with inputs \(X = S\) and \(Y = R\)
\(J-K\) Flip-Flop with inputs \(X = J\) and \(Y = K\)
\(J-K\) Flip-Flop with inputs \(X = K\) and \(Y = J\)
questions.explanation:
From the given combinational logic circuit feeding into the \(D\) flip-flop, the boolean expression for the input \(D\) can be derived from the logic gates:
  • The top AND gate has inputs \(\overline{X}\) and \(Z\). Its output is \(\overline{X}\,Z\).
  • The bottom AND gate has inputs \(Y\) and \(\overline{Z}\). Its output is \(Y\,\overline{Z}\).
  • The OR gate combines these two outputs: \[D = \overline{X}\,Z + Y\,\overline{Z}\]
For a \(D\) flip-flop, the next-state characteristic equation is: \[Z_{n+1} = D\] Substituting the expression for \(D\): \[Z_{n+1} = Y\,\overline{Z_n} + \overline{X}\,Z_n\] The standard characteristic equation of a \(J\text{-}K\) flip-flop with next state \(Q_{n+1}\) and current state \(Q_n\) is given by: \[Q_{n+1} = J\,\overline{Q_n} + \overline{K}\,Q_n\] By mapping \(Z\) to \(Q\), we compare the two equations:
  • Comparing the coefficients of \(\overline{Z_n}\) (or \(\overline{Q_n}\)): \(J = Y \implies Y = J\)
  • Comparing the coefficients of \(Z_n\) (or \(Q_n\)): \(\overline{K} = \overline{X} \implies K = X \implies X = K\)
Thus, the circuit acts as a \(J\text{-}K\) flip-flop with inputs \(X = K\) and \(Y = J\). \[\boxed{\text{(D)}\; J - K \text{ Flip-Flop with inputs } X = K \text{ and } Y = J}\]
Key points
  • D Flip-Flop Characteristic Equation: \(Q_{n+1} = D\)
  • J-K Flip-Flop Characteristic Equation: \(Q_{n+1} = J\overline{Q}_n + \overline{K}Q_n\)
  • Any flip-flop can be converted into another by finding the required combinational logic expression for its excitation inputs.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Be careful with the inversion bubble at the input of the top AND gate. It is attached to \(X\), resulting in \(\overline{X}\), not \(\overline{Z}\).
  • When comparing with the standard \(J\text{-}K\) equation, remember that the coefficient of \(Q_n\) is \(\overline{K}\), so \(\overline{X} = \overline{K}\) leads to \(X = K\).

questions.question: For the 4 bit DAC shown in Figure, the output voltage \(v_o\) is
questions.explanation:
The given circuit consists of a 4-bit \(R\text{-}2R\) ladder network connected to a non-inverting operational amplifier configuration. Determine the binary input from the ladder connections
Let the ground terminal represent Logic-0 and the \(1\,\text{V}\) source represent Logic-1. Looking at the ladder configuration from the most significant bit (MSB) closest to the op-amp non-inverting terminal to the least significant bit (LSB):
  • \(b_3\) (MSB, closest to \(V^+\)) is connected to \(1\,\text{V} \rightarrow 1\)
  • \(b_2\) is connected to Ground \(\rightarrow 0\)
  • \(b_1\) is connected to \(1\,\text{V} \rightarrow 1\)
  • \(b_0\) (LSB, farthest from \(V^+\)) is connected to Ground \(\rightarrow 0\)
Thus, the 4-bit binary input sequence \((b_3 b_2 b_1 b_0)_2 = (1010)_2\). The decimal equivalent of this binary value is: \[D = 1 \times 2^3 + 0 \times 2^2 + 1 \times 2^1 + 0 \times 2^0 = 10\] Find the non-inverting node voltage \(V^+\)
For a standard \(R\text{-}2R\) ladder with reference voltage \(V_{ref}\), the voltage \(V^+\) at the non-inverting input terminal is given by: \[V^+ = \frac{V_{ref}}{2^n} \times D\] Given \(V_{ref} = 1\,\text{V}\) and \(n = 4\): \[V^+ = \frac{1}{2^4} \times 10 = \frac{10}{16}\,\text{V}\] Calculate the output voltage \(V_o\)
The operational amplifier is in a non-inverting configuration with feedback resistor \(R_f = 7\,\text{k}\Omega\) and input resistor \(R_1 = 1\,\text{k}\Omega\). The output voltage is expressed as: \[V_o = \left( 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1} \right) V^+\] Substituting the given resistor values and \(V^+\): \[V_o = \left( 1 + \frac{7\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} \right) \times \frac{10}{16}\] \[V_o = 8 \times \frac{10}{16} = 5\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) } 5\text{ V}}\]
Key points
  • The output expression for an \(n\)-bit \(R\text{-}2R\) ladder DAC connected to a non-inverting amplifier is: \[V_o = \left( 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1} \right) \times \frac{V_{ref}}{2^n} \times D\] where \(D\) is the decimal equivalent of the binary pattern applied.
  • In an \(R\text{-}2R\) network, the bit closest to the amplifier terminal always represents the Most Significant Bit (MSB).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Carefully trace the binary inputs starting from the terminal nearest to the Op-Amp as the MSB (\(b_{n-1}\)) to avoid reversing the binary sequence to \((0101)_2\).

questions.question: The number of comparators in a \(4\text{ bit}\) flash ADC is
questions.explanation:
Given that the number of bits is \(n = 4\). The number of comparators required for an \(n\)-bit flash type Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) is given by the formula: \[N = 2^n - 1\] Substituting \(n = 4\) into the formula: \[N = 2^4 - 1 = 16 - 1 = 15\] Thus, the number of comparators required is \(15\). \[\boxed{\text{(C) } 15}\]
Key points
  • For an \(n\)-bit flash ADC:
    • Number of comparators \(= 2^n - 1\)
    • Number of resistors \(= 2^n\)
    • Number of decoder input lines \(= 2^n - 1\)
  • Flash ADC is the fastest type of ADC because conversion takes place simultaneously through parallel comparators.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the number of comparators (\(2^n - 1\)) with the number of resistors or total resolution states (\(2^n\)).

questions.question: An 8 bit successive approximation analog to digital converter has full scale reading of \(2.55\text{ V}\) and its conversion time for an analog input of \(1\text{ V}\) is \(20\ \mu\text{s}\). The conversion for a \(2\text{ V}\) input will be
questions.explanation:
A Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter operates using a binary search algorithm to determine the digital equivalent of an analog input voltage. The conversion time (\(T_{conv}\)) for an \(n\)-bit SAR ADC depends exclusively on the total number of bits (\(n\)) and the internal clock period (\(T_{CLK}\)): \[T_{conv} = n \cdot T_{CLK}\] Because the binary search process evaluates each bit position sequentially from the Most Significant Bit (MSB) to the Least Significant Bit (LSB), the total number of clock cycles required remains constant. It does not fluctuate with variations in the magnitude or amplitude of the analog input signal. Given parameters:
  • Conversion time for an analog input of \(1\,\text{V} = 20\,\mu\text{s}\)
Since the conversion mechanism is independent of the input level, the conversion time for an analog input of \(2\,\text{V}\) remains identically \(20\,\mu\text{s}\). \[\boxed{\text{(B) } 20\,\mu\text{s}}\]
Key points
  • SAR Conversion Characteristics: A key benefit of the SAR architecture over a counter-controlled or dual-slope ADC is its fixed, predictable conversion speed (\(n\) clock cycles for an \(n\)-bit output) regardless of the input voltage amplitude.

To clear the accumulator (set \(A = 00\text{H}\)) with minimum execution time, we compare common alternative approaches:
  1. XRA A (Exclusive OR accumulator with itself):
    • Size: \(1\) Byte
    • Machine Cycles: \(1\) (Opcode Fetch)
    • T-states: \(4\) T-states
  2. SUB A (Subtract accumulator from itself):
    • Size: \(1\) Byte
    • Machine Cycles: \(1\) (Opcode Fetch)
    • T-states: \(4\) T-states
  3. MVI A, 00H (Move immediate value \(00\text{H}\) to accumulator):
    • Size: \(2\) Bytes
    • Machine Cycles: \(2\) (Opcode Fetch + Memory Read)
    • T-states: \(7\) T-states (\(4 + 3\))
Both XRA A and SUB A execute in the absolute minimum possible time of \(4\) T-states. \[\boxed{\text{XRA A (or SUB A)}}\]
Key points
  • Register-to-register logical or arithmetic instructions targeting the accumulator require only \(1\) machine cycle (\(4\) T-states) because no supplementary memory operands are read.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The contents of Register (B) and Accumulator (A) of 8085 microprocessor are \(49\text{H}\) and \(3\text{AH}\) respectively. The contents of A and the status of carry flag (CY) and sign flag (S) after executing SUB B instructions are
questions.explanation:
The execution of the SUB B instruction performs subtraction by adding the \(2\)'s complement of register \(B\)'s content to the accumulator (\(A\)): \[A \leftarrow A - B = A + (\text{2's complement of } B)\] Given values:
  • \(A = 3\text{AH} = 0011\,1010_2\)
  • \(B = 49\text{H} = 0100\,1001_2\)
Step 1: Compute the 2's complement of B
\[\text{1's complement of } B = 1011\,0110_2\] \[\text{2's complement of } B = 1011\,0110_2 + 1 = 1011\,0111_2\] Step 2: Add to Accumulator
\(A\):\(0011\,1010_2\)
+ \(\text{2's complement of } B\):\(1011\,0111_2\)
Result:0\(1111\,0001_2\)
Step 3: Flag Analysis
  • Accumulator (\(A\)): The binary result \(1111\,0001_2\) corresponds to \(\text{F1H}\).
  • Carry Flag (\(\text{CY}\)): During addition using 2's complement, an internal carry out of MSB is \(0\). In the 8085 architecture, for subtraction operations, the carry flag is the complement of this addition carry: \[\text{CY} = \overline{\text{Addition Carry}} = \overline{0} = 1\] This indicates that a borrow was required because \(A < B\).
  • Sign Flag (\(\text{S}\)): The most significant bit (MSB) of the result is \(1\), so \(\text{S} = 1\) (negative result).
\[\boxed{\text{(A) } A = \text{F1}, \text{CY} = 1, S = 1}\]
Key points
  • For subtraction (SUB, SUI), the 8085 complements the final carry bit of the adder hardware to represent the true borrow state.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In the 8085 microprocessor, the RST6 instruction transfers the program execution to the following location
questions.explanation:
The restart instruction RST n is a \(1\)-byte software interrupt instruction in the 8085 microprocessor. It transfers the program execution to a specific vector address located in the lower memory area. The vector address for any restart instruction RST n (where \(n\) ranges from \(0\) to \(7\)) is calculated by multiplying the interrupt vector number \(n\) by \(8\) bytes: \[\text{Vector Address (Decimal)} = n \times 8\] Given \(n = 6\) for the RST 6 instruction: \[\text{Vector Address (Decimal)} = 6 \times 8 = 48_{10}\] Now, converting the decimal address \(48_{10}\) to its \(16\)-bit hexadecimal equivalent: \[48_{10} = 3 \times 16 + 0 = 30\text{H}\] Thus, the execution transfers to the memory location \(0030\text{H}\) (written as \(30\text{H}\)). \[\boxed{\text{(A) } 30\text{ H}}\]
Key points
  • Each software interrupt vector location is separated by exactly \(8\) bytes in memory because historical interrupt service routines (ISR) could use a jump instruction to redirect elsewhere.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The number of hardware interrupts (which require an external signal to interrupt) present in an 8085 microprocessor are
questions.explanation:
The 8085 microprocessor consists of physical pins dedicated to receiving external signaling requests to interrupt regular program execution. These are classified structurally as hardware interrupts. There are exactly \(5\) hardware interrupt pins on the 8085 microprocessor package, listed below in decreasing order of their operational priority:
  1. TRAP: Non-maskable highest priority edge-and-level triggered interrupt.
  2. RST 7.5: Maskable edge-triggered interrupt.
  3. RST 6.5: Maskable level-triggered interrupt.
  4. RST 5.5: Maskable level-triggered interrupt.
  5. INTR: Maskable lowest priority level-triggered general-purpose interrupt.
Therefore, the total number of hardware interrupts present is \(5\). \[\boxed{\text{(C) } 5}\]
Key points
  • Software interrupts (RST 0 to RST 7) are initiated by instructions written within code, whereas hardware interrupts are triggered by external peripheral signals applied directly to the CPU pins.

questions.explanation: The system's characteristic equation is: \[s^2 + 3s + G = 0\] Comparing with the standard second-order system equation \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^2 = 0\): \[\omega_{n} = \sqrt{G}, \quad 2\xi\omega_{n} = 3 \implies \xi = \frac{3}{2\sqrt{G}}\] The peak overshoot from the step response graph is \(M_{p} = 0.1\) (\(10\%\)): \[M_{p} = \exp\left(\frac{-\pi\xi}{\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}}\right) = 0.1 \implies \xi \approx 0.5912 \approx 0.6\] \[\sqrt{G} = \frac{3}{2 \times 0.6} = 2.5 \implies G = 2.5^2 = \boxed{6.25}\]

questions.question: An amplifier with resistive negative feedback has two left half plane poles in its open-loop transfer function. The amplifier
options: will always be unstable at high frequency.
will be stable for all frequency.
may be unstable, depending on the feedback factor.
questions.explanation:
For the given data, the block diagram of the system is shown below: With a resistive negative feedback network having a feedback factor \(K\), the closed-loop transfer function is given by: \[T(s) = \frac{G(s)}{1 + K \cdot G(s)} = \frac{A_0}{(1 + s\tau_1)(1 + s\tau_2) + K A_0}\] Expanding the denominator gives the characteristic equation: \[s^2 \tau_1 \tau_2 + s(\tau_1 + \tau_2) + 1 + K A_0 = 0\] Since \(\tau_1 > 0\), \(\tau_2 > 0\), and \(K A_0 > -1\), all coefficients of this second-order characteristic equation remain strictly positive for any positive feedback factor \(K\). Consequently, both roots will always lie in the left half of the \(s\)-plane. \[\boxed{\text{(B) \ will be stable for all frequency}}\]
Key points
A second-order system with negative feedback never becomes unstable or goes into sustained oscillations because the maximum phase shift contributed by two poles is strictly less than \(180^\circ\).

questions.question: In a digital communication system employing Frequency Shift Keying (FSK), the \(0\) and \(1\) bit are represented by sine waves of \(10\ \text{kHz}\) and \(25\ \text{kHz}\) respectively. These waveforms will be orthogonal for a bit interval of
questions.explanation:
Theory:
Two FSK waveforms are orthogonal when their inner product over one bit interval is zero. For coherent BFSK, an equivalent shortcut is that the bit duration is the reciprocal of the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two frequencies. Given \[f_1 = 25~\text{kHz}, \qquad f_2 = 10~\text{kHz}\]Orthogonality condition: \[\int_{0}^{T_b} \cos(2\pi f_1 t)\, \cos(2\pi f_2 t)\,dt =0\]Using the shortcut, \[f_0=\gcd(f_1,f_2) =\gcd(25,10)\,\text{kHz} =5~\text{kHz}\]Hence, \[T_b=\frac{1}{f_0} =\frac{1}{5\times10^3}\] \[T_b =2\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}\] \[\boxed{(B)T_b=200~\mu\text{s}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: In an FM system, a carrier of \(100\text{MHz}\) is modulated by a sinusoidal signal of \(5\text{kHz}\). The bandwidth by Carson's approximation is \(1\text{MHz}\).If \(y(t)=\text{(modulated waveform)}^3\), then by using Carson's approximation, the bandwidth of \(y(t)\) around \(300\text{MHz}\) and the spacing of spectral components are, respectively.
questions.explanation:
Theory: Raising an FM signal to the \(n^{\text{th}}\) power multiplies the carrier frequency and frequency deviation by \(n\), while the modulating frequency remains unchanged. Adjacent spectral components are separated by\[f_m=5~\text{kHz}.\]Using Carson's rule,\[BW=2(\Delta f+f_m)=1~\text{MHz}.\]Hence,\[\Delta f+f_m=500~\text{kHz}\]\[\Delta f=500-5=495~\text{kHz}.\]Since\[y(t)=\big(\text{FM signal}\big)^3,\]the non-linearity triples the carrier frequency and frequency deviation:\[(\Delta f)_{\text{new}}=3\times495=1485~\text{kHz},\]\[(f_c)_{\text{new}}=300~\text{MHz}.\]The modulating frequency remains\[f_m=5~\text{kHz}.\]Therefore,\[BW_{\text{new}} = 2\left(1485+5\right)\times10^3 = 2.98~\text{MHz} \approx 3~\text{MHz}.\]The spacing between adjacent spectral components remains\[5~\text{kHz}.\]Hence,\[\boxed{(A) 3~\text{MHz},\;5~\text{kHz}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not multiply the modulating frequency by the non-linearity order.
  • Only the carrier frequency and frequency deviation scale by the factor \(n\).
  • Apply Carson's rule after computing the new frequency deviation.
  • Spectral spacing in FM is always equal to the modulating frequency.

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A message \(m(t)\) band limited to the frequency \(f_m\) has a power of \(P_m\). The power of the output signal in the figure is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Theory: Multiplication with a coherent carrier followed by low-pass filtering retains only the baseband component scaled by the phase mismatch factor. The multiplier output is\[m(t)\cos\omega_0t\cdot\cos(\omega_0t+\theta).\]Using\[\cos A\cos B=\frac{1}{2}\left[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)\right],\]we get\[=\frac{m(t)}{2}\left[\cos(2\omega_0t+\theta)+\cos\theta\right].\]The ideal LPF removes the high-frequency term, therefore\[v_o(t)=\frac{m(t)}{2}\cos\theta.\]Hence,\[P_{\text{out}} =\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int v_o^2(t)\,dt\]\[=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T} \int\left(\frac{m(t)}{2}\cos\theta\right)^2dt\]\[=\frac{\cos^2\theta}{4} \left[\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int m^2(t)\,dt\right].\]Since\[P_m=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int m^2(t)\,dt,\] \[\boxed{(D) P_{\text{out}}=\frac{P_m\cos^2\theta}{4}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget the factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\) obtained from the product-to-sum identity.
  • The LPF removes the \(2\omega_0\) component completely.
  • Power is proportional to the square of amplitude, hence \(\cos^2\theta\) appears instead of \(\cos\theta\).
  • Use the given message power \(P_m\) directly after evaluating the average of \(m^2(t)\).

questions.question: The amplitude modulated wave form\[s(t)=A_c\left[1+K_am(t)\right]\cos\omega_ct\]is fed to an ideal envelope detector. The maximum magnitude of \(K_am(t)\) is greater than 1. Which of the following could be the detector output?
questions.explanation:
Theory: When an AM signal is overmodulated, the envelope detector follows the magnitude of the envelope instead of its signed value. The AM signal is\[s(t)=A_c[1+K_am(t)]\cos\omega_ct.\]Since \[|K_am(t)|>1,\]overmodulation occurs. Hence, the envelope detector produces\[\boxed{(C) \left|A_c\left[1+K_am(t)\right]\right|}.\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Envelope detectors cannot preserve the sign after envelope inversion.
  • Overmodulation occurs when \(|K_am(t)|>1\).
  • Envelope is always the magnitude of the signal envelope.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Two coaxial cables \(1\) and \(2\) are filled with different dielectric constants \(\epsilon_{r1}\) and \(\epsilon_{r2}\) respectively. The ratio of wavelengths in the two cables, \((\lambda_1/\lambda_2)\) is
questions.explanation: The velocity of a wave in a medium is defined by the permeability (\(\mu\)) and permittivity (\(\epsilon\)) of the medium. For two different media, the velocities \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) are given by: \[v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_1 \epsilon_1}}\] \[v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_2 \epsilon_2}}\] Taking the ratio of the two velocities (assuming \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_0\) for non-magnetic media): \[\frac{v_1}{v_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_2}{\epsilon_1}}\] Given that the frequency of operation (\(f\)) remains constant for a wave passing between media, and using the relationship \(v = f\lambda\), we have \(v \propto \lambda\). Therefore: \[\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}\] Substituting the permittivity values in terms of relative permittivity \(\epsilon_r\) (\(\epsilon = \epsilon_0 \epsilon_r\)): \[\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_2}{\epsilon_1}} = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_0 \epsilon_{r2}}{\epsilon_0 \epsilon_{r1}}}\] \[\boxed{(B):\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_{r2}}{\epsilon_{r1}}}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A uniform plane wave in air impinges at \(45^\circ\) angle on a lossless dielectric material with dielectric constant \(\epsilon_r\). The transmitted wave propagates in a \(30^\circ\) direction with respect to the normal. The value of \(\epsilon_r\) is
questions.explanation: The problem requires finding the relative permittivity (\(\epsilon_{r}\)) using Snell's Law for an electromagnetic wave propagating between two media. Given the ratio of the transmission angle (\(\theta_{t}\)) to the incidence angle (\(\theta_{i}\)): \[\frac{\sin \theta_{t}}{\sin \theta_{i}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\epsilon_{r}}}\] Substituting the given values, where \(\theta_{t} = 30^{\circ}\) and \(\theta_{i} = 45^{\circ}\): \[\frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 45^{\circ}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}\] Using the trigonometric values \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 1/2\) and \(\sin 45^{\circ} = 1/\sqrt{2}\): \[\frac{1/2}{1/\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}\] Simplifying the left side: \[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}\] Squaring both sides to solve for \(\epsilon_{r}\): \[\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{\epsilon_{r}}\] \[\boxed{(C) :\epsilon_{r} = 2}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A TEM wave is incident normally upon a perfect conductor. The \(E\) and \(H\) fields at the boundary will be respectively
questions.explanation:
The reflection coefficient for electric fields (\(\Gamma_{E}\)) at an interface between two media is given by the ratio of the intrinsic impedances. For an interface between a general medium (with impedance \(\eta = \sqrt{j\omega\mu/\sigma}\)) and free space (with impedance \(\eta_{0} \simeq 120\pi\)), the formula is: \[\Gamma_{E} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma}} - 120\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma}} + 120\pi}\] When the medium is a good conductor, the conductivity \(\sigma\) is very large, such that the intrinsic impedance \(\eta \simeq 0\). Substituting this into the equation: \[\Gamma_{E} \simeq \frac{0 - 120\pi}{0 + 120\pi} = -1\] This result indicates that the electric field reflects with a phase shift of \(180^{\circ}\) (completely out of phase). Applying boundary conditions at the conductor surface: \[E_{r} - E_{i} = 0 \implies E_{tang} = 0\] Conversely, for the magnetic field \(H\), the reflection is in phase, leading to: \[\boxed{(C):H_{r} + H_{i} = 2H_{t}, \text{ where } H_{tang} \text{ is maximum}}\]
Key points
  • For a perfect conductor (\(\sigma \to \infty\)), the intrinsic impedance \(\eta \to 0\).
  • The tangential component of the electric field \(E_{tang}\) must vanish at the surface of a perfect conductor.
  • The tangential component of the magnetic field \(H_{tang}\) is doubled at the surface of a perfect conductor due to the induced surface current.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The magnitude of the open-circuit and short-circuit input impedance of a transmission line are \(100 \, \Omega\) and \(25 \, \Omega\) respectively. The characteristic impedance of the line is,
questions.explanation: To determine the characteristic impedance (\(Z_{0}\)) of a transmission line, we use the open-circuit impedance (\(Z_{OC}\)) and the short-circuit impedance (\(Z_{SC}\)) as follows: \[Z_{0} = \sqrt{Z_{OC} \cdot Z_{SC}}\] Given values: \[Z_{OC} = 100\,\Omega\] \[Z_{SC} = 25\,\Omega\] Substituting these values into the formula: \[Z_{0} = \sqrt{100 \times 25}\] \[Z_{0} = \sqrt{2500}\] \[Z_{0} = 50\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{(B):50}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A rectangular waveguide has dimensions \(1\text{ cm} \times 0.5\text{ cm}\). Its cut-off frequency is
questions.explanation: To determine the cut-off frequency (\(f_{c}\)) for the \(TE_{10}\) dominant mode in a rectangular waveguide, we use the given waveguide dimension \(a = 1\,\text{cm}\). The cut-off wavelength (\(\lambda_{c}\)) for the \(TE_{10}\) mode is given by: \[\lambda_{c} = 2a = 2 \times 1\,\text{cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\] The cut-off frequency (\(f_{c}\)) is then calculated using the speed of light (\(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\)): \[f_{c} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{c}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}}{2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}}\] \[f_{c} = 1.5 \times 10^{10}\,\text{Hz} = 15\,\text{GHz}\] \[\boxed{(C):15\,\text{GHz}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: For an \(8\) feet (\(2.4\text{ m}\)) parabolic dish antenna operating at \(4\text{ GHz}\), the minimum distance required for far field measurement is closest to
questions.explanation:
To determine the minimum distance required for the Fraunhofer region (far-field) measurements, we use the standard criterion for antenna performance. The Fraunhofer distance \(r\) is given by the inequality: \[r > \frac{2D^2}{\lambda}\] First, calculate the wavelength \(\lambda\) using the speed of light \(c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}\) and the given frequency \(f = 4 \times 10^9\,\text{Hz}\): \[\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{4 \times 10^9} = 0.075\,\text{m}\] Given the maximum antenna dimension \(D = 2.4\,\text{m}\), we substitute these values into the formula: \[r = \frac{2 \times (2.4\,\text{m})^2}{0.075\,\text{m}}\] \[r = \frac{2 \times 5.76}{0.075}\] \[r = \frac{11.52}{0.075} = 153.6\,\text{m}\] \[\boxed{(D):150}\]
Key points
  • The Fraunhofer zone (far-field) is where the radiation pattern of an antenna becomes independent of the distance from the antenna.
  • In this region, the wave appears as a plane wave.
  • The criterion \(r > \frac{2D^2}{\lambda}\) ensures that the phase error across the aperture is less than \(\pi/8\) radians.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the near-field (Fresnel zone) with the far-field (Fraunhofer zone), as measurements in the near-field are dominated by reactive components (\(1/r^2\) and \(1/r^3\) terms).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: If the diameter of a \(\lambda/2\) dipole antenna is increased from \(\dfrac{\lambda}{100}\) to \(\dfrac{\lambda}{50}\), then its
questions.explanation:
The efficiency of an antenna is a critical parameter that directly influences its gain. It is defined as the ratio of radiated power to the total input power. The efficiency \(\eta_{r}\) is given by: \[\eta_{r} = \frac{P_{rad}}{P_{in}} = \frac{R_{rad}}{R_{rad} + R_{l}}\] Where:
  • \(R_{rad}\) is the radiation resistance.
  • \(R_{l}\) is the ohmic loss resistance.
The loss resistance \(R_{l}\) is determined by the physical dimensions of the antenna wire, expressed as: \[R_{l} = \frac{\rho l}{\text{Area}}\] Where \(\rho\) is the resistivity and \(l\) is the length of the wire. As the diameter of the dipole antenna wire increases, the cross-sectional area (\(\text{Area} = \pi r^2\)) increases. Consequently, for a constant length and material, an increase in diameter leads to a decrease in the loss resistance \(R_{l}\). Given that the diameter increases (e.g., from \(\lambda/100\) to \(\lambda/50\)), \(R_{l}\) decreases. Referring to the efficiency formula: \[\eta_{r} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{R_{l}}{R_{rad}}}\] As \(R_{l}\) decreases, the denominator decreases, causing the overall efficiency \(\eta_{r}\) to increase. Since antenna gain \(G\) is related to directivity \(D\) and efficiency \(\eta_{r}\) by \(G = \eta_{r} D\), an increase in efficiency results in an increase in the antenna gain. \[\boxed{(C):\text{Gain increases}}\]
Key points
  • Antenna Efficiency: Measures how much of the input power is actually radiated versus dissipated as heat.
  • Loss Resistance (\(R_{l}\)): Represents losses due to finite conductivity of the antenna material.
  • Relationship: Increasing the conductor diameter reduces ohmic losses, thereby improving the radiation efficiency of the antenna.
